screens.title: Introduction to Error Handling: Exceptions
screens.subtitle: Why C++ exceptions matter, the core mechanics, and practical patterns you will use today.

narration.text: In real programs things go wrong: files disappear, networks drop, or inputs are invalid. This lesson introduces exceptions in C++ as a structured way to detect and handle those unexpected conditions. You will learn the core keywords — try, throw, and catch — see how the runtime moves control to handlers, and understand why separating error handling from main logic makes code clearer and safer. We'll examine standard exception types you can reuse, and show how to write custom exception classes when an application needs richer error data. You will also learn common pitfalls to avoid, such as catching by value and throwing from destructors, and we will preview the connection to RAII for resource safety. By the end you will be able to read and write guarded code that reports useful messages and keeps your program in a known state. Which error case would you prioritize first in your last project, and how would a thrown exception improve its reliability?

keyIdea.text: Exceptions let you separate normal logic from error handling using try, throw, and catch so programs can recover or terminate cleanly with informative messages.

Introduction to Error Handling: Exceptions

Learn the why and how of C++ exceptions, use standard types, design custom exceptions, and avoid common mistakes that lead to crashes or sliced objects.

Orientation

We will start with mechanics, inspect standard exceptions, build a custom exception class, and finish with practical advice for resource-safe code.

Why this matters

Unhandled errors can crash your application or corrupt data. Exceptions let you centralize error handling and keep business logic readable.

screens.title: Learning Objectives
screens.subtitle: Skills you'll build in this chapter

narration.text: Over these screens you will develop a precise, usable skill set for handling runtime errors in C++. First, you will understand why robust error handling is essential: it prevents crashes, protects data, and provides clearer failure modes that are easier to test. Second, you will learn the core syntax and behavior of try, throw, and catch so you can control non-local transfers of execution. Third, you will identify and use standard exception types like runtime error and bad alloc to represent common problems without reinventing messages. Fourth, you'll begin designing custom exception classes to carry domain data and message text for your application's errors. Each objective has a short practice focus so you can verify competency by writing small guarded functions. These skills matter because they make systems resilient and maintainable. As you progress, ask yourself which errors should be signaled with exceptions versus simple return codes, and how exception safety affects resource cleanup.

You will practice writing guarded functions that throw meaningful exceptions rather than returning ambiguous codes, and you will practice catching by const reference so derived information is preserved. You will also set up small tests that provoke std::bad_alloc, out of range, and invalid argument conditions to confirm your handlers run as expected. screens.title: Why exception-based error handling?
screens.subtitle: Understand the purpose and trade-offs of using exceptions in C++

narration.text: Exceptions provide a mechanism to separate error-handling logic from the happy path, letting you write clearer, more maintainable code. Instead of peppering return-code checks after every call, exceptions allow you to signal a failure at the site where it occurs and handle it at an appropriate higher level. This separation matters in medium and large programs because it reduces boilerplate and centralizes recovery strategies. A concrete example is a file reader that encounters a missing file: throwing an exception allows caller code to decide whether to retry, supply a default, or report a fatal error, instead of relying on obscure return values. A common misconception is that exceptions always slow performance or are only for catastrophic failures. In practice, exceptions give better structure for exceptional, not expected, control flows; they are meant for unusual conditions. Another trade-off is that exception paths must be tested and resources must be released; this is why RAII and deterministic destructors are fundamental. As a takeaway, ask yourself whether an error is truly exceptional — if it is, prefer an exception; if it is expected, consider normal return handling. How will your design ensure resources are released when exceptions occur?

keyIdea.title: Definition
keyIdea.text: Exceptions signal exceptional conditions and let calling code decide how to recover, keeping normal logic uncluttered.

content.html:
Core Concept

Why use exceptions?

Exceptions keep error paths separate from normal code, enabling clearer logic and centralized recovery decisions.

Concrete example
A file reader throws if the file is missing; higher-level code chooses to retry, prompt the user, or abort cleanly.
Common misconception
Exceptions are not for ordinary control flow or expected, frequent conditions. They are for exceptional, infrequent errors.
Why it matters
Centralized handling improves reliability and maintainability. Combined with RAII, exceptions lead to safe cleanup even when control jumps out of a scope.
Key Takeaway

Use exceptions for unexpected failures and design your code so resources are released deterministically when exceptions occur.

Analogy
Think of normal code as the main road and exceptions as a detour sign. When something blocks the road, the detour redirects control to handlers that know how to navigate the new route.
Try
Wrap code that might fail.
Throw
Signal an error by throwing an exception object.
Catch
Handle the specific or general error and decide recovery steps.
RAII note
Use RAII for resource cleanup to ensure exceptions don't leak resources; RAII is the next chapter topic.

screens.title: Try, Throw, Catch: Control transfer
screens.subtitle: How exceptions change execution flow and how handlers are selected

narration.text: The try-throw-catch sequence defines a non-local transfer of control. When code inside a try block throws an exception object, execution of that block stops immediately. The runtime then searches outward for a catch block whose type matches the thrown object or a base class of that object. Matching is based on type compatibility: a catch that accepts a given derived type will be chosen before a catch that accepts a base class, so order matters. If no handler is found in the current function, the search continues up the call stack, unwinding stack frames and running destructors for local objects. A concrete example is a divide function that throws when the denominator is zero; the call site can catch std::runtime_error specifically or use a general std::exception fallback. A common misconception is that catch-all patterns are safe everywhere. In reality, catch-all provides no typed information and should be used sparingly, typically at top-level boundaries to prevent termination while logging diagnostic details. As a takeaway, design handlers at levels that can make appropriate recovery decisions, and prefer specific catches to keep behavior explicit.

keyIdea.title: Process
keyIdea.text: Throwing an exception halts the current block, unwinds the stack, and transfers control to the first compatible catch handler.

content.html:
Process Flow

Throwing and handler selection

Try block
→
Throw an exception
→
Catch handler
Stack unwinding
As propagation moves out of a function, local destructors are run. This ensures RAII-managed resources are released before reaching a handler.
Handler order matters
Place specific types before general ones. If a derived exception is thrown and a base type is caught by value first, derived information can be lost.
Example scenario
Call divide; if the function throws a runtime error for division by zero, the runtime will find a matching catch or continue unwinding up the stack until one is found or program termination occurs.
Common mistake
Using catch-all early hides the actual error type and makes correct recovery harder.
Key Takeaway

Throw to signal errors, let the runtime unwind safely, and catch where you can make the right decision based on the exception type.

screens.title: Divide example: throwing and catching
screens.subtitle: Read the divide function example and see control transfer in action

narration.text: Let's walk through the divide example to make the mechanics concrete. The function checks the denominator and throws a runtime error with a readable message when division by zero is detected. In main, the try block calls divide twice. The first call returns normally and prints a result, while the second call triggers a throw. Execution immediately leaves the try block and searches for the first matching catch. If a catch for runtime error exists, it executes the handler which can inspect the message through a standard method and log or recover. Notice the skipped line after the throwing call: code after the point of throw in the try block is not executed. A frequent student error is to rely on subsequent lines in the try block to run after a throw; they do not. Another important point is that catching by const reference avoids copying and preserves polymorphic type. As a takeaway, test both success and throw paths. Try altering the code to throw a derived exception and see which catch runs to reinforce how matching works. Divide example: throwing and catching means throwing inside a function aborts normal execution there and transfers control to the first compatible catch higher up the stack.. In practical terms, read the divide function example and see control transfer in action. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Code example
keyIdea.text: Throwing inside a function aborts normal execution there and transfers control to the first compatible catch higher up the stack.

content.html:
Code Walkthrough

divide function

Read the code to see how a runtime error is thrown on invalid input and handled by specific catch blocks in main.
#include <iostream>
#include <stdexcept>

double divide(double numerator, double denominator) {
  if (denominator == 0) {
    throw std::runtime_error("Error: Division by zero is not allowed.");
  }
  return numerator / denominator;
}

int main() {
  try {
    double result1 = divide(10.0, 2.0);
    std::cout << "10.0 / 2.0 = " << result1 << std::endl;

    double result2 = divide(5.0, 0.0); // This will throw an exception
    std::cout << "This line will not be reached." << std::endl;
  } catch (const std::runtime_error& e) {
    std::cerr << "Caught an exception: " << e.what() << std::endl;
  } catch (const std::exception& e) {
    std::cerr << "Caught a general standard exception: " << e.what() << std::endl;
  } catch (...) {
    std::cerr << "Caught an unknown exception type." << std::endl;
  }

  std::cout << "Program continues after exception handling." << std::endl;
  return 0;
}
Explanation
  • When divide throws, the remaining lines in the try block are skipped and control moves to the first matching catch.
  • Using catch by const reference preserves the exception object's type and avoids copying.
  • Specific catches (runtime_error) should appear before broader ones (std::exception) to allow tailored handling.
Check your understanding
Change the thrown type and observe which catch block runs to see matching and ordering in practice.
Key Takeaway

Test both normal and exceptional paths; catching by const reference preserves information and avoids slicing.

screens.title: Standard exception types
screens.subtitle: Common classes in the std::exception hierarchy and when to use them

narration.text: The C++ standard library offers a hierarchy of exception classes rooted at std::exception. Key types you will encounter include std::bad_alloc for memory allocation failures, std::out_of_range for invalid container indexing, std::invalid_argument for bad inputs, std::logic_error for logic errors, and std::runtime_error for runtime problems that don't fit a more specific category. Using predefined types has two benefits: they provide standardized names and messages, and they integrate with existing tooling that looks for these types. A concrete example: if a function requests a large allocation that fails, throwing std::bad_alloc lets callers catch that particular resource problem and perhaps try a smaller allocation. A common mistake is to throw strings or raw integers; prefer throwing exception objects derived from std::exception for compatibility and informative messages. As a takeaway, when in doubt choose the most specific standard exception that describes the problem, and use catch const std::exception& as a fallback to handle unknown standard errors. Which standard type best expresses the last error you handled in a project? Standard exception types means use specific std::exception-derived types for common problems and reserve general catches for fallback behavior.. In practical terms, common classes in the std::exception hierarchy and when to use them. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Standard Exceptions
keyIdea.text: Use specific std::exception-derived types for common problems and reserve general catches for fallback behavior.

content.html:
Definition

Std exception types

std::bad_alloc
Used when memory allocation fails; handlers can try alternative strategies or fail gracefully.
std::out_of_range
Signals invalid container access like an index outside bounds.
std::invalid_argument
Indicates the caller passed an unacceptable argument value.
std::runtime_error
A general runtime problem when no more specific type suits the error.
Practical guidance
  • Prefer specific standard types that communicate intent and let callers choose appropriate recovery.
  • Use std::exception as a fallback handler to log unexpected standard errors.
  • Avoid throwing plain strings; std::exception derivatives provide polymorphism and a standard what() method.
Key Takeaway

Choose the most precise standard exception that fits the failure and reserve generic catches for top-level logging or shutdown handling.

screens.title: Custom exceptions: InsufficientFundsExample
screens.subtitle: Design a custom exception that stores extra data and use it in a transaction example

narration.text: Custom exceptions let your domain code attach structured data to errors. The example InsufficientFundsException derives from std::runtime_error and stores fields for current balance and requested withdrawal so handlers can inspect numeric context and decide what to do. In withdraw, the code checks for negative withdrawals and throws an invalid argument if needed, and throws the custom exception when the balance is insufficient. In main, catching the custom type by const reference allows you to call getters for current balance and requested amount, enabling informative logs or UI messages. A common beginner error is to derive from std::exception but forget to call the base constructor with a message; include a clear message to aid debugging. Another pitfall is to throw heavy objects by value without proper move semantics; keep exceptions lean or rely on base types. As a practical exercise, modify the custom exception to include a small error code and see how a handler can switch behavior based on that code. What additional context would help a caller decide whether to prompt the user or abort? Custom exceptions: InsufficientFundsExample means derive from std::exception or a suitable subclass and include domain data to let handlers make informed recovery decisions.. In practical terms, design a custom exception that stores extra data and use it in a transaction example. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Custom Exceptions
keyIdea.text: Derive from std::exception or a suitable subclass and include domain data to let handlers make informed recovery decisions.

content.html:
Custom Exception

InsufficientFundsException

#include <iostream>
#include <stdexcept>

class InsufficientFundsException : public std::runtime_error {
public:
  InsufficientFundsException(double balance, double withdrawalAmount)
    : std::runtime_error("Insufficient funds for withdrawal."),
      currentBalance(balance), requestedAmount(withdrawalAmount) {}

  double getBalance() const { return currentBalance; }
  double getRequestedAmount() const { return requestedAmount; }

private:
  double currentBalance;
  double requestedAmount;
};

void withdraw(double& balance, double amount) {
  if (amount < 0) {
    throw std::invalid_argument("Withdrawal amount cannot be negative.");
  }
  if (balance < amount) {
    throw InsufficientFundsException(balance, amount);
  }
  balance -= amount;
}
Explanation
  • Derive from a standard exception class for interoperability and to expose what() for messages.
  • Store minimal domain data in the exception so handlers can make informed decisions without extra queries.
  • Always catch custom exceptions by const reference to preserve data and avoid slicing.
Analogy
A custom exception is like an error report with extra fields: it tells handlers not only that something failed, but exactly why and with what values.
Key Takeaway

Keep custom exceptions focused, derive from the standard hierarchy, and provide accessors so handlers can act on context.

screens.title: Catching: by value vs by const reference
screens.subtitle: Understand object slicing and why const reference is the recommended pattern

narration.text: A common beginner mistake is catching exception objects by value instead of by const reference. Catching by value creates a copy of the thrown object, which can be inefficient and, worse, can cause object slicing when a derived exception is thrown and caught as a base type by value. Object slicing removes derived-class-specific data and behavior, so handlers lose context such as custom fields or methods. By catching with a const reference, you avoid copies and preserve the exact dynamic type of the thrown object so polymorphic behavior and accessors remain available. For example, if InsufficientFundsException is thrown and you catch std::runtime_error by value, the balance and requested amount are lost. Some developers think copying is harmless; it is not, especially when exceptions carry extra data. As a practical rule: catch exceptions using catch (const SomeExceptionType& e). This preserves information and improves performance. As a closing question, consider which handlers in your codebase need full derived-type information and which can safely use broader types. Catching: by value vs by const reference means catch exceptions by const reference to avoid copying and object slicing, preserving type and data.. In practical terms, understand object slicing and why const reference is the recommended pattern. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Catch pattern
keyIdea.text: Catch exceptions by const reference to avoid copying and object slicing, preserving type and data.

content.html:
Comparison

By value vs By const reference

Catching by value
Copies the exception object; risk of slicing and extra cost.
Catching by const reference
Preserves the dynamic type, avoids copying, and prevents slicing.
Common mistake
Catching by value using a base type can strip derived data, making handlers blind to the full error context.
Concrete scenario
If InsufficientFundsException is thrown, handlers that catch the specific custom type by const reference can read current balance and requested amount. If a handler catches std::runtime_error by value first, that numeric context is gone.
Key Takeaway

Adopt catch (const T& e) as your default to preserve information and avoid slicing or unnecessary copies.

screens.title: Throwing from destructors and noexcept
screens.subtitle: Why throwing from a destructor can call std::terminate and what to do instead

narration.text: Throwing exceptions from destructors is hazardous because destructors commonly run during stack unwinding. If a destructor throws while another exception is already active, the C++ runtime will call terminate, ending the program immediately. To avoid this, prefer designs where destructors do not throw. If a cleanup operation can fail, handle the failure inside the destructor: log the error, swallow it, or store an error state that the owning code can inspect later. Modern C++ makes destructors implicitly noexcept by default to discourage throwing. A common pattern is to perform critical cleanup in a function that returns an error code or throws, but call that function from contexts where exceptions are safe, not from the destructor itself. Another approach is to use RAII objects whose destructors are simple and cannot fail, and move complex operations to explicit methods that the caller invokes before destruction. As a takeaway, design destructors to be noexcept and test failure paths to ensure they do not allow a second exception to escape during unwinding. Which of your classes perform complex work in destructors, and how might you refactor them to avoid throws?

keyIdea.title: Destructor safety
keyIdea.text: Avoid throwing from destructors; prefer noexcept destructors and move fallible cleanup to explicit functions or safe RAII patterns.

content.html:
Definition

Destructors and exceptions

If a destructor throws during stack unwinding while another exception is active, the runtime will call terminate. To prevent this, destructors should not allow exceptions to escape.

Safe patterns
Make destructors noexcept and perform fallible cleanup in explicit methods that the caller can call where exceptions are acceptable.
RAII note
RAII still applies: prefer simple resource wrappers whose destructors do not throw.
Concrete advice
  • Catch and handle errors inside destructors rather than letting them propagate.
  • Prefer explicit close or flush methods that report errors to callers before destruction.
  • Make destructors noexcept to document the intent and avoid implicit termination on failures.
Key Takeaway

Design destructors to avoid throwing; surface fallible cleanup through explicit, testable operations.

screens.title: Activity: getUserAge() with custom InvalidAgeException
screens.subtitle: Plan and design the function and custom exception required by the hands-on activity

narration.text: This hands-on activity asks you to write a getUserAge function that validates user input and throws a custom InvalidAgeException for invalid scenarios. The custom exception should derive from std::runtime_error and include messages for non-numeric input and out-of-range values, for example less than zero or greater than 120. The function must read from standard input, detect stream failures or non-numeric data, clear and discard bad input appropriately, and then either return a valid age or throw the custom exception. In main, call getUserAge inside a try block and provide catch handlers for InvalidAgeException, stream-related errors like stream failure, and a general std::exception fallback. A key implementation detail is to avoid swallowing stream state silently: after a failed extraction clear the state and discard the invalid token before retrying or throwing. A useful test is to feed non-numeric input and an out-of-range number to verify the correct exception and message are produced. This exercise practices designing specific exceptions, input validation, and safe top-level handling. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. screens.title: Catch ordering and catch-all use
screens.subtitle: Why ordering catch blocks matters and when catch(...) is appropriate

narration.text: The order of catch blocks determines which handler executes when multiple catches could match a thrown exception. Place specific exception types first, then more general types. If you reverse that order and catch a base class before a derived class, the derived handler will never run. For example, catching std::runtime_error before std::invalid_argument may prevent the more specific invalid argument handler from executing. The catch-all handler catch(...) can intercept any thrown value, including non-standard types, but it provides no typed information, so it is best used sparingly at an application boundary for logging, cleanup, or to ensure graceful termination. A misconception is to use catch-all everywhere to avoid crashes; this hides real bugs and removes the ability to perform tailored recovery. As a good practice, handle specific conditions where you can recover, and reserve catch(...) for the top-level to log and shutdown safely. Reflect on where your program should fail fast versus where it should attempt to recover. Catch ordering and catch-all use means place specific catch handlers before general ones; use catch(...) only at high-level boundaries for logging or safe termination.. In practical terms, why ordering catch blocks matters and when catch(...) is appropriate. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Handler Ordering
keyIdea.text: Place specific catch handlers before general ones; use catch(...) only at high-level boundaries for logging or safe termination.

content.html:
Comparison

Specific vs General handlers

Correct order
Place derived handlers first, then base class handlers, then catch(...).
When to use catch(...)
At top-level only: log diagnostic data, release critical resources, and perform controlled shutdown or restart logic.
Example implication
If you catch a broad type early, you may mask actionable details that a more specific handler could use to recover or retry safely.
Key Takeaway

Order handlers from specific to general and keep catch-all handlers limited to boundary-level logging and shutdown responsibilities.

screens.title: Testing exception paths and resource cleanup
screens.subtitle: Make sure your handlers actually run and resources are released during failures

narration.text: Testing exception paths is essential because exceptional behavior is often untested and the source of subtle bugs. Create unit tests that intentionally provoke exceptions — invalid inputs, forced allocation failures, or simulated resource errors — and assert that handlers run and resources are cleaned up. For resource safety, use RAII so destructors release resources deterministically during stack unwinding. When a test triggers an exception, verify that no leaks occur and that any persisted state remains consistent. A common oversight is only testing the happy path; add tests that call code under failure modes and check logs, returned error states, or restored invariants. For custom exceptions, test that accessor methods return the expected diagnostic values. As a final check, run top-level scenarios that use catch-all handlers to observe graceful shutdown behavior. The takeaway: cover both normal and exceptional flows in tests so your code behaves predictably under real failures. Testing exception paths and resource cleanup means intentionally test error paths and verify resource cleanup using raii to ensure robust behavior under failures.. In practical terms, make sure your handlers actually run and resources are released during failures. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Testing
keyIdea.text: Intentionally test error paths and verify resource cleanup using RAII to ensure robust behavior under failures.

content.html:
Best Practice

Test exception paths

Write tests that trigger thrown exceptions and assert handlers run and state remains valid. Use RAII to ensure deterministic cleanup during unwinding.
Test ideas
Simulate input errors, force allocation failures where possible, and assert cleanup and logged diagnostics.
RAII verification
Confirm destructors release resources when exceptions unwind the stack, preventing leaks and inconsistent state.
Practical checklist
  1. Write unit tests that provoke each exception type your code can throw.
  2. Assert that handlers perform expected logging, state changes, or retries.
  3. Run memory/RAII checks to ensure no resource leaks occur during failure.
Key Takeaway

Include exceptional scenarios in your test suite and verify that resources are released correctly during unwinding.
